title: C. Itoh & Co. (America) Inc. v. Jordan International Co.
summary: A seller’s acknowledgment that expressly conditioned acceptance on the buyer’s assent to its additional terms formed no contract through the writings, but delivery and payment formed one under § 2-207(3) whose terms were those on which the writings agreed plus the Code’s gap-fillers; the seller’s unagreed arbitration clause was neither, so it dropped out.
notes:
Court: Seventh Circuit (1977).

552 F.2d 1228 (7th Cir. 1977). The dispute arose after Itoh's own customer, Riverview Steel, alleged defects and refused payment; the Seventh Circuit rejected the district court's judicial-economy ground (the Federal Arbitration Act requires a stay whenever an arbitration agreement exists) but affirmed because no agreement to arbitrate was ever formed.

sections.Parties: C. Itoh & Co. (America) Inc., the steel buyer, was the plaintiff and appellee, suing for allegedly defective steel and late delivery. The Jordan International Company, the seller, was the defendant and appellant, contending that the dispute had to be arbitrated under its acknowledgment form and seeking a stay pending arbitration. Judge Sprecher wrote for the Seventh Circuit on April 4, 1977.
sections.Material Facts: Itoh sent Jordan a purchase order for steel coils. Jordan responded with an acknowledgment form whose language expressly conditioned the seller’s acceptance on the buyer’s assent to the additional or different terms on its face and reverse, and directed the buyer to notify the seller at once if the terms were unacceptable. One reverse-side provision required arbitration; Itoh’s purchase order contained no arbitration clause and Itoh never assented to the added terms. The writings therefore did not agree on arbitration. Jordan nevertheless delivered the steel and Itoh paid for it. Itoh later complained that the steel was defective and had arrived late; the dispute surfaced after Itoh’s own customer, Riverview Steel, alleged defects and refused payment.
sections.Procedural History: Itoh sued Jordan for the alleged defects and late delivery. Jordan moved to stay the proceedings pending arbitration under its acknowledgment, and the district court denied the motion on a judicial-economy ground. Jordan appealed. The Seventh Circuit rejected the district court’s rationale, because the Federal Arbitration Act requires a stay whenever an arbitration agreement exists, but affirmed the denial because no agreement to arbitrate had ever been formed. This account follows the casebook’s excerpt of the opinion (Farnsworth, seventh edition, pp. 199–201); the brief did not independently verify the full reported text.
sections.Issue: When a seller expressly conditions acceptance on the buyer’s assent to additional terms, the buyer does not assent, and both parties nevertheless perform, does § 2-207(3) create a contract? If so, can the seller’s arbitration clause become one of its terms through the buyer’s receipt and payment or through the provision for supplementary Code terms?
sections.Holding: Jordan’s acknowledgment satisfied the expressly-conditional proviso of § 2-207(1), so the exchange of writings formed no contract and the acknowledgment operated as a counteroffer. The parties’ performance nevertheless established a contract under § 2-207(3), whose terms were those on which the writings agreed together with supplementary terms incorporated under the Code. The writings did not agree on arbitration and Article 2 supplies no arbitration term as a gap-filler, so the clause was excluded; delivery and payment proved the sale without proving assent to the added clause. The denial of the stay was affirmed.
sections.Reasoning: Jordan’s form used the condition Dorton’s forms lacked: it tied acceptance expressly to the buyer’s assent to additional or different terms, which prevented formation through the writings unless that condition was met. The failure of the writings did not end the matter, because § 2-207(3) recognizes contracts demonstrated by both parties’ conduct: Jordan delivered and Itoh paid, objective evidence of a sale the Code would not treat as nonexistent merely because the forms failed to match. The same subsection fixed the terms. Its agreed-terms rule excluded the arbitration clause because the buyer’s order never agreed to it. Nor could the clause return as a supplementary term, since that phrase refers to Article 2’s standardized gap-fillers, which complete a contract with default obligations rather than importing disputed boilerplate the agreed-terms rule has just excluded. A seller that chooses an expressly conditional form gains freedom from commitment through the writings and can withhold delivery until it obtains assent; if it delivers without assent, it accepts the risk that the conduct-based contract will omit its unagreed terms.

priorVersions.summary: An expressly conditional acknowledgment followed by performance created a § 2-207(3) contract without the seller’s unmatched arbitration clause.
priorVersions.notes:
Court: Seventh Circuit (1977).

The shared factual motif with Dorton is insufficient to equate the outcomes. The wording and function of the condition determine which statutory route is used.

sections.Parties: Itoh, the buyer of steel coils, sued Jordan, the seller, alleging defective and late goods. Jordan sought arbitration.
sections.Material Facts: Itoh sent a purchase order. Jordan’s acknowledgment explicitly conditioned its acceptance on the buyer’s assent to additional or different terms, including arbitration. The parties delivered, received, and paid for the steel without obtaining the required assent to that term.
sections.Procedural History: The district court denied Jordan’s motion to stay proceedings pending arbitration. The Seventh Circuit affirmed.
sections.Issue: When the writings fail to form a contract because acceptance is expressly conditional, does later performance adopt the seller’s arbitration clause or form a contract under § 2-207(3)?
sections.Holding: The contract arose by the parties’ conduct under subsection (3). Its terms included the writings’ agreed terms and the Code’s supplementary terms; arbitration was not one of them.
sections.Reasoning: The condition kept subsection (1) from completing a contract through the exchanged writings. Performance nevertheless recognized a sale. Treating delivery and payment as automatic assent to the conditional form would restore the last-shot advantage the provision addresses. A disputed additional term cannot reenter as a “supplementary term” when the Code’s gap-fillers do not supply it. A seller can protect its insistence on arbitration by securing assent before delivery; choosing to perform without it carries the corresponding risk.

learning.why: The contrast with Dorton is precise: different wording changes the statutory route, and that route changes how the contract’s terms are determined.

topics.battle-forms: Subsection (3) governs the contract recognized by conduct.
topics.conditional-acceptance: Express language prevented formation under subsection (1).
topics.conduct-contract: Shipment, receipt, and payment established a sale.
topics.gap-fillers: Supplementary terms come from the Code rather than the unmatched form.
topics.arbitration: No agreed or Code-supplied arbitration term existed.
topics.assent: Performance recognized a sale without accepting every proposed clause.
topics.ucc207-conduct: C. Itoh is the leading application of 2-207(3): performance by both parties forms the contract when the writings do not.
topics.gap-filling: The court limited supplementary terms under 2-207(3) to Code gap-fillers, excluding the arbitration clause.
topics.arbitration-formation: Whether the arbitration clause became part of the contract was resolved as a formation question under 2-207.
